events.excerpt: Executive summary Ethereum’s upcoming enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS) introduces new ways for validators to participate in block-building markets. Most importantly, it enables builders to compete directly for block proposals, with payments guaranteed by the Ethereum protocol, reducing the need for trusted intermediaries. This proposal seeks to preserve the principles of Lido’s existing MEV Policy while adapting it to ePBS: maximizing rewards for stakers, supporting open and competitive block-building markets, and ensuring that Node Operators (NOs) do not favor particular builders or withhold MEV rewards. Following the discussion in Lido’s call for an updated MEV policy . It proposes a two-track approach: 1. An open, permissionless market where Lido validators can accept bids from any builder meeting Ethereum’s protocol requirements, provided payments are guaranteed by the protocol. 2. A vetted market where builders and intermediaries offering additional payments outside Ethereum’s guarantees must be approved through Lido’s Allowed List. Both tracks apply regardless of how a bid arrives: via p2p, a direct connection, or through one of the available sidecars. APR is maximized as operators can source from the full market; MEV hiding remains detectable because every bid

events.excerpt: Hello, I’ve opened a PR for a new opcode, SLOTDURATION . It pushes the duration of the current slot, in milliseconds, onto the stack. PR: Add EIP: SLOTDURATION Opcode by Amxx · Pull Request #12619 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub Open questions: Current duration or historical lookup? The draft returns the current duration. The Rationale describes an alternative where the opcode takes a slot number and returns the duration in effect at that slot, or 0 for future slots. That would let contracts like Lido’s compute correct timestamps across duration changes. The cost is that the execution layer would have to keep the duration schedule. Which is more useful? Milliseconds. I chose ms to match SLOT_DURATION_MS and to support L2s with 100–250 ms block times. Any objections? 0 for “no regular interval.” Is this the right sentinel for on-demand chains, and should L1 execution clients still reject 0 ? Execution-layer decoupling. EIP-8198 deliberately keeps the execution layer unaware of the slot duration. The draft keeps the EL config-free, but it does add a header field. Is that acceptable to the EIP-8198 authors and to client teams? 3 posts - 3 participants Read full topic
events.headline: EIP-8484: SLOTDURATION Opcode

events.excerpt: CometBFT v0.38.25 can’t read an ML-DSA public key. Its PubKeyFromProto knows Ed25519 and secp256k1, and its MaxSignatureSize is 64 bytes, while an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309. That’s the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs, and the v29.1.0 release candidate from Monday keeps it. The Quarterly says post-quantum consensus keys shipped with SDK v0.55 and CometBFT v0.40, and that the Hub moves to v30 once ibc-go carries v0.55. Before any chain lets its validators use those keys, I wanted to know what breaks on the other side of its IBC connections, so I read the rotation code and the light clients. The SDK docs already say every counterparty must upgrade before the first validator rotates. This is what I’d add to that. v0.38.26 is enough for a Go counterparty The docs ask counterparties for CometBFT v0.40. On the 0.38 line there’s a smaller step. v0.38.26 (13 August, PR 6028 ) backports only ML-DSA decoding and verification, “for the purposes of verification of IBC connections with counterparty chains that are on v0.40”, and raises MaxSignatureSize to 3,309. It doesn’t let the chain itself use the key. So a chain on SDK v0.53 doesn’t need the v0.55 migration for its own clients of an ML-DSA chain, a patch release on the line it’s on covers it. What a counterparty runs is in its /cosmos/base/t

events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. The draft applies the same freshness requirement to installation, replacement, and zero-address revocation. Installed delegations remain in effect after their author
events.headline: EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations

For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences. AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast. Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials. Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time. AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours. And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. events.excerpt: Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it. I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet. Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors. Two weeks and a slow prototype Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school. That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow. events.excerpt: In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind , I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system. Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany: Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change. In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm. We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. events.excerpt: [Final Report] zkArb SDK — Dev Tooling on One and Stylus (D.A.O. Season 3) Hi everyone, this is the final report for zkArb SDK , funded through the Arbitrum D.A.O. Grant Program Season 3, Dev Tooling on One and Stylus domain. All seven milestones have been delivered. Summary zkArb SDK is a zero-setup toolkit that turns the full zero-knowledge proof lifecycle on Arbitrum into a few CLI commands and one JavaScript function. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. What happened XCM programs are meant to be transactional. That is, when a program fails, none of the state changes from that program are applied. There was a bug present that did not follow this behavior in certain circumstances. The issue was first reported to Parity through its
events.headline: XCM Incident Review: What happened and what we learned

events.excerpt: A growing class of protocols needs to persist one tiny fact per event, forever: this nullifier is spent, this nonce is used, this session share is settled. Privacy pools write a nullifier per withdrawal. Unordered nonce schemes (Permit2’s nonceBitmap , EIP-4337-style two-dimensional nonces) write replay flags because they cannot guarantee sequenced nonces. Machine-scale settlement (DePIN connectivity, bandwidth, compute) writes a mark per settled session. Call all of it what it is: replay protection, and its cost is pure storage. ZK batching has made the compute side nearly free: one proof verifies thousands of signatures or membership checks at flat cost. The flags are what no longer compress. The progression every protocol rediscovers. Worst case, and still the most common shape: mapping(bytes32 => bool) used; // one flag, one slot // every flag: ~22,100 gas (20,000 zero-to-nonzero + 2,100 cold access), state forever This is what nullifier sets look like: the key is a hash, so no two flags ever share a slot, and nothing amortizes. First optimization, 256 flags per word, when flag ids are dense: mapping(uint256 => uint256) bitmap; // key = flagId >> 8, bit = flagId & 255 // first flag in a word: ~22,100; each later flag: ~5,000 (2,100 access + 2,900 reset, own tx) This is Permit
events.headline: Storage-optimized replay protection: from hash => bool to packed flag lanes, and can the protocol offer better?

events.excerpt: TL;DR: XCMv3 will be removed in polkadot-sdk stable2612 (release 2026-12-17, ingestion by fellowship runtimes only after that). Once system chains upgrade, they will no longer send or accept v3 messages. If your chain or your app still uses v3, you need to move to v4 or v5 before then. Check your chain on the dashboard: XCM Versions . XCMv5 was merged in November 2024: XCM v5 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #4826 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub . A PR removing v3 ( Remove XCMv3 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #13629 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub ) will ship in stable2612 , scheduled for 2026-12-17 . After that, system parachains and any other runtime can adopt it. Allowing for runtime releases and governance, expect the first chains to drop v3 in early 2027. Once a chain drops v3, it can’t decode v3 messages sent to it and can’t downgrade outgoing messages to v3. XCM between that chain and any other chain still on v3 will fail. To help, I built a dashboard ( XCM Versions ) showing each chains’ XCM version. Click a chain to see suggested action items. The main ones are: Code: move XCM programs and types to v4+. This is mostly renames (e.g. dropping the Multi prefix). Raw v3 types in storage don’t need migrating because the encoding is the same, but stored Versioned*

events.excerpt: When I last wrote about our DNS propagation pipeline in 2022 , the Zone Builder received about 250 DNS record changes per second. Today it receives about 700, nearly three times as many, plus about 100 other events, such as zone setting changes. However, the number of events was never the real problem. The problem was the kind of work some of those events needed, and how that work grows with the size of a zone. Some zones now hold more than 20 million records, and we expect them to keep growing toward hundreds of millions. Each event starts a clock that measures how long it takes us to turn that change into data our authoritative DNS servers can use. We call that work a build. A build reads the current database state, converts it into the format used at the edge, and writes any changes to Quicksilver . In 2022, per-record builds were 150 times faster than full builds on average. On a test zone with one million records, per-record builds were 4,250 times faster. We ended that post with the obvious next step: do the same thing for zone settings. Why doesn't the Zone Builder just rebuild the setting that changed? It should, and that is where we ended up. However, proving when it was safe took most of the work. A record event identifies what changed. A zone event can come from many C
